summary.headline: High returns and a 10% yield, but profit is falling back from a one-off boost: fair at Rs 97, buy at Rs 87.50 or lower
summary.text: Commercial Credit and Finance (COCR.N0000) is a Kandy-based leasing and finance company that is cheap on paper and pays a large dividend, and at Rs 96.70 it trades a little below my fair value of about Rs 103. Profit for 2025/26 jumped 59% to Rs 9.75bn (EPS Rs 30.66, ROE 30%), but about Rs 5bn of that came from releasing old loan-loss provisions as bad loans were collected or written off (gross non-performing loans fell from 26% to 4.7%). The September 2026 half-year shows the more normal level: profit down 10% to Rs 3.79bn (EPS Rs 11.92), because provisions are being charged again and borrowing costs rose 34%. It trades at 0.83x NAV of Rs 115.97 and about 3.3x trailing earnings, and paid Rs 10 a share for 2025/26 (a 10% yield). With a 19.5% required return for a smaller, BBB+-rated lender, four methods put fair value at about Rs 103. I'd buy at up to Rs 87.50 and treat Rs 77 or less as a strong buy. The business passes three of the four tests (strong returns, very high capital, good dividend), but profit is not steady: it halved in 2022/23 and 2025/26 leaned on one-off provision releases.

highlights.title: Six months to September 2026 (group, unaudited)
highlights.text: Profit after tax fell 10% to Rs 3.79bn; EPS Rs 11.92 against Rs 13.30. Second-quarter profit fell 18% to Rs 1.72bn (EPS Rs 5.41).

highlights.title: What drove it
highlights.text: Net interest income rose 10% to Rs 11.6bn, but interest costs rose 34%. Loan-loss provisions were a Rs 846mn charge against a Rs 957mn release a year earlier, a Rs 1.8bn swing. Other operating costs rose 37%. The TVS Lanka associate added Rs 705mn.

highlights.title: 2025/26 (audited)
highlights.text: Profit rose 59% to Rs 9.75bn (EPS Rs 30.66, ROE 30.1%), helped by a Rs 4.96bn release of loan-loss provisions as gross non-performing loans fell from 26.07% to 4.71% through collections and write-offs. Without the release, profit would have been roughly Rs 7–8bn (my estimate).

highlights.title: Balance sheet
highlights.text: Leases and loans Rs 95.6bn at September, down 3.5% from March (loans and receivables down Rs 4.7bn). Deposits up 9% to Rs 60.4bn. Core capital 27.0% at March, nearly three times the 10% minimum.

highlights.title: Dividend and shareholders
highlights.text: Rs 10 a share for 2025/26 (Rs 3 interim + Rs 7 final), Rs 3.18bn paid in April–September 2026, up from Rs 6. Group Lease Holdings (in liquidation), which held 30%, is no longer among the top 20 shareholders at September; public holding rose to 49%.

models.name: Justified price to book
models.comment: Book value Rs 115.97 × (ROE − growth) ÷ (cost of equity − growth): long-run ROE 16% / 19% / 22%.

models.name: Dividend model
models.comment: The strictest method: Rs 8 / 10 / 11 next year, growing 5% / 8% / 10% for five years, then 5% / 6% / 7%.

models.name: Residual income
models.comment: Used instead of a cash-flow DCF: book value plus profit above the required return, ROE fading from 19–22% to the long-run level over ten years, 40% payout.

modelsNote: A finance company's cash flows are mostly lending and deposits, so instead of a cash-flow DCF I used residual income and a justified price-to-book, alongside P/E and dividends.

scenarios.common: Government bonds about 12.4% (November 2026) plus about 7 points for a smaller, BBB+-rated leasing company with a history of bad loans (1.5 points more than Central Finance). H1 EPS is Rs 11.92, so base 2026/27 EPS of Rs 24 needs the second half at about the first-half pace.

sensitivity.title: Residual income base case, Rs per share
sensitivity.note: Rs 96.70 is what a 19.5% cost of equity gives if long-run ROE settles at 16%.

buyPlan.note: About Rs 45,300 in total, against Rs 48,350 for 500 shares at Rs 96.70.
buyPlan.realism: The share fell from Rs 122 to Rs 96.50 in July–September 2026, and traded as low as Rs 89.40 in the September 2025 quarter. Rs 87.50 is about 10% below the September close, which looks reachable if profit keeps falling; Rs 77 would need a broad sell-off.

higher: Loan book growing again without new bad loans (it shrank 3.5% in the half-year).
Provision charges staying small, so ROE holds above 20%.
A stable new holder for the former Group Lease 30% stake, or a wider float lifting the market's multiple.
Lower interest rates reducing funding costs.
lower: Non-performing loans rising again after the 2025/26 clean-up.
Funding costs continuing to rise faster than lending rates (interest expense up 34%).
A smaller dividend as profit falls back to normal.
Related-party or governance concerns at a family-controlled lender.
Weaker profit from the TVS Lanka associate (Rs 705mn in the half-year).

notes.disclaimer: These are estimates from the 2025/26 annual report and the unaudited interim report to 30 September 2026. The price is the 30 September 2026 close because a newer CSE close wasn't available to this run, so check the current price before ordering. This is analysis, not personal financial advice.

fullText:
Summary: Commercial Credit and Finance (COCR.N0000) is a Kandy-based leasing and finance company that is cheap on paper and pays a large dividend, and at Rs 96.70 it trades a little below my fair value of about Rs 103. Profit for 2025/26 jumped 59% to Rs 9.75bn (EPS Rs 30.66, ROE 30%), but about Rs 5bn of that came from releasing old loan-loss provisions as bad loans were collected or written off (gross non-performing loans fell from 26% to 4.7%). The September 2026 half-year shows the more normal level: profit down 10% to Rs 3.79bn (EPS Rs 11.92), because provisions are being charged again and borrowing costs rose 34%. It trades at 0.83x NAV of Rs 115.97 and about 3.3x trailing earnings, and paid Rs 10 a share for 2025/26 (a 10% yield). With a 19.5% required return for a smaller, BBB+-rated lender, four methods put fair value at about Rs 103. I'd buy at up to Rs 87.50 and treat Rs 77 or less as a strong buy. The business passes three of the four tests (strong returns, very high capital, good dividend), but profit is not steady: it halved in 2022/23 and 2025/26 leaned on one-off provision releases.

Price and key figures
Price: Rs 96.70, the last traded price on 30 September 2026 (interim report). July–September 2026 range Rs 96.50–122.00.
Six months to September 2026 (group, unaudited): profit after tax Rs 3.79bn, down 10%; EPS Rs 11.92 against Rs 13.30. Net interest income up 10%, interest expense up 34%, provision charge Rs 846mn against a Rs 957mn release, other costs up 37%, TVS Lanka associate Rs 705mn.
2025/26 (group, audited): profit Rs 9.75bn (up 59%), EPS Rs 30.66, ROE 30.1%, NAV Rs 114.04. Provision release Rs 4.96bn. Gross NPL 4.71% (26.07%), core capital 27.02%. Dividend Rs 10 (Rs 3 interim + Rs 7 final).
Balance sheet at September 2026: leases and loans Rs 95.6bn (down 3.5%), deposits Rs 60.4bn (up 9%), bank borrowing Rs 27.2bn, equity Rs 36.9bn, NAV Rs 115.97.

Valuation table (Rs per share)
Method | Bear | Base | Bull | Weighted
Justified price to book | 79.7 | 111.7 | 158.1 | 111.4
P/E | 77.0 | 108.0 | 143.0 | 105.7
Dividend model | 50.0 | 78.4 | 109.2 | 76.0
Residual income | 79.6 | 118.3 | 176.7 | 118.4
Average | 71.6 | 104.1 | 146.8 | 103

Assumptions (bear / base / bull)
Cost of equity 21% / 19.5% / 18%; long-run ROE 16% / 19% / 22%; growth 5% / 6% / 7%; 2026/27 EPS 22 × 3.5 / 24 × 4.5 / 26 × 5.5; next dividend Rs 8 / 10 / 11 growing 5% / 8% / 10% for five years.

Business tests: 3 of 4 passed (fails steady profit); a good business priced between fair value and the buy price: watch list.

500-share plan
200 shares up to Rs 103, 150 up to Rs 87.50, 150 up to Rs 77: about Rs 45,300 in total.

Uncertain: the price is the 30 September close (no newer CSE close was available to this run). The annual report gives a 2025/26 price range of Rs 103–140, which doesn't match the Rs 89.40 low the September 2025 interim gave for that quarter. Earlier year-end prices (for P/E history) weren't in the reports read.
